title: Inheritance and polymorphism
description: Base and derived classes, virtual and override, abstract classes, interfaces, and when not to inherit.

content.title: Inheritance: "is a"
content.body:
A class can inherit from another one: class Cat : Animal { }. Cat (the derived class) gets the members of Animal (the base class), and can add its own. A cat is an animal, so a Cat can be used wherever an Animal is expected.

In C#, a class has exactly one base class; when you do not write one, it is object. A class can also implement any number of interfaces.

A method marked virtual can be replaced in a derived class with override. Which version runs is decided by the real type of the object at run time: that is polymorphism.

content.question: How many base classes can a C# class inherit from?

choices.text: Exactly one (object when none is written), plus any number of interfaces

content.explanation: C# has single inheritance for classes, which avoids the ambiguities of multiple inheritance. Interfaces cover the need to have several "abilities".
The variable's type is Animal, but the object is a Cat. With virtual and override, the object's real type decides: Cat.Speak runs. That is polymorphism.
new hides the base method instead of overriding it. The call goes through a variable of type Animal, so Animal.Speak runs. Only override gives polymorphism; this trap is why hiding is rare.
base.Speak() calls the version of the base class. It lets a derived class extend the behaviour instead of replacing it completely.

content.title: Abstract classes and interfaces
content.body:
An abstract class cannot be created with new. It is a base made to be completed: its abstract members have no body, and each derived class must override them.

An interface is a contract: a list of members a class promises to provide, such as interface IFlyable { void Fly(); }. A class inherits from one class at most, but can implement many interfaces.

sealed does the opposite of abstract: no class can inherit from a sealed class.

choices.text: It does not compile: an abstract class cannot be instantiated
It creates a shape whose area is 0
It compiles, but Area() throws an exception
It creates an object of the first class that inherits from Shape

content.explanation: Shape is incomplete: Area has no body. You create concrete derived classes instead, such as new Circle(2), and use them as Shapes.

content.question: A Duck can fly and swim. A Plane can fly. What is the best design?

choices.text: An IFlyable interface implemented by both Duck and Plane
Copy the Fly method into both classes

content.explanation: A plane is not a duck, and a duck is not a plane, so inheritance is wrong here. They only share an ability, which is exactly what an interface describes.

content.question: Someone wrote class Car : Engine { } so that a car can Start(). What is the problem?

choices.text: A car is not an engine, it has an engine: Car should hold an Engine field
Nothing, it is a good use of inheritance
Engine should inherit from Car instead
C# does not allow a class to inherit from another class

content.explanation: Inheritance means "is a". For "has a", use composition: class Car { private readonly Engine engine; }. Prefer composition over inheritance when in doubt.

content.question: What does sealed class Token { } prevent?

choices.text: Other classes from inheriting from Token
Changing the fields of a Token

content.explanation: sealed closes a class to inheritance. It protects designs that were not made to be extended.

content.instructions: Match each concept with its meaning.

pairs.definition: The class another class inherits from
A class that inherits from another one
Allows derived classes to override a method
Replaces a virtual method in a derived class
Cannot be instantiated; made to be inherited from
A contract of members that a class promises to provide
